Stedfastly
STED-fast-lee
adv.
From stedfast (the Authorized Version’s spelling of steadfast), Saxon stedefaest — fixed in place, from stede, a place, and faest, fast. Webster 1828: with fixedness or firmness; with constancy or resolution.

Biblical Definition

Stedfastly means fixed in place, and Scripture uses it of the four things the church did, of the Lord’s face set toward Jerusalem, of a dying man’s gaze, and of a widow’s settled resolve. Of the first church: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers (Acts 2:42). Four things, and nothing else is listed — the apostolic teaching, the common life, the Lord’s table, and prayer. Of the Lord: when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), which begins the long central section of Luke’s Gospel and describes a man walking deliberately toward His own execution. Of Stephen, in the moment of his death: being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God (Acts 7:55) — and the Son of man is standing, not seated, to receive him. And of Ruth, whose fixedness ended an argument: When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her (Ruth 1:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STEDFASTLY as with fixedness or firmness; with constancy; with steadiness of mind or of the eye; resolutely and without wavering.

expand to see more

STEDFASTLY, adv. — With fixedness or firmness; with constancy; resolutely.

With a fixed and unwavering gaze; as, to look stedfastly upon a thing.

STEDFAST, a. — Fast fixed; firm; not to be moved from its place or purpose.

Constant; resolute; not fickle or wavering; as, stedfast in the faith.

From Saxon stede, a place, and faest, fast — literally, fixed in place.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Luke 9:51 — "And it came to pass, when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem,"

Acts 7:55 — "But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,"

Ruth 1:18 — "When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her."

Modern Corruption

Acts 2:42 lists exactly four things the first church continued stedfastly in, and the modern congregation that has added a great deal to that list while quietly subtracting from it should notice which of the four is usually the first to go.

expand to see more

The four are the apostles’ doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers. That is the whole inventory. It is worth asking any congregation which of the four its calendar actually protects. Doctrine is often reduced to a doctrinal statement nobody reads and a preaching diet that avoids the harder texts. Fellowship becomes attendance. The breaking of bread — whether one reads it of the Lord’s Supper, the common meal, or both together — is frequently quarterly. And the prayer meeting is, in most churches, the least attended gathering of the week, which is a plain statement about what the congregation believes accomplishes anything. The regulative principle is not a fussy restriction; it is the instinct that what God appointed is sufficient and that additions crowd out the appointed things.

Luke 9:51 sets the word in its most solemn use. Christ stedfastly set his face toward Jerusalem when the time came — a Hebrew idiom for immovable resolve, borrowed from Isaiah 50:7, therefore have I set my face like a flint. He was not swept along by events, arrested by surprise, or overtaken by a plot. He walked toward the cross deliberately, at the hour appointed, having told His disciples three times what waited there. Acts 7:55 shows the fruit of the same steadiness in a man about to be stoned: full of the Holy Ghost, looking stedfastly into heaven, seeing Jesus standing. That is what fixedness produces at the end, and it is why Paul urges the Corinthians to be stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue steadfastly, to persist in; atenizo (G816), to fix the eyes upon, to gaze intently; sterizo (G4741), to fix, to establish; Hebrew amets (H553), to be firm.

expand to see more

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to attend constantly, to persevere in; they continued stedfastly (Acts 2:42).

Greek atenizo (G816) — to gaze fixedly; Stephen looked up stedfastly into heaven (Acts 7:55).

Greek sterizo (G4741) — to set fast, to establish; he stedfastly set his face (Luke 9:51).

Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled, steadfast; be ye stedfast, unmoveable (1 Corinthians 15:58).

Hebrew amets (H553) — to be alert, firm, determined; she was stedfastly minded (Ruth 1:18).

Usage

"They continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine (Acts 2:42) — four things, and no others listed."

"He stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51) — a man walking deliberately toward His own execution."

"Looked up stedfastly into heaven… and Jesus standing (Acts 7:55) — and He is standing, not seated, to receive him."
